calls.reason: The Times documented substantial text reproduction, which OpenAI acknowledged could occur. Linklaters also reports a court finding infringement in generated Ultraman images, supporting the broad capability claim.

CopyCat demonstrates character generation from name-free prompts, but its deliberate tests do not establish infringement by unsuspecting users. The packet supports the risk more clearly than the full claim.

The Munich ruling supports continuing infringement, and CopyCat shows unintended character-generation risks. Neither establishes how often unrequested infringement occurs or its dependence on a new provenance architecture.

Tom's Hardware independently generated recognizable Mario and Sonic images through Bing. It did not show matches to particular source images, leaving the stronger claim of near-verbatim reproduction unclear.
The Register documents a temporary Disney-name ban and a replacement restriction that reportedly worked. It does not demonstrate a failure of the relevant name-blocking safeguard.

The Times exhibit shows copied text without a notice in the displayed completion, but lacks complete interface records. OpenAI's description of safety checks does not establish whether delivered outputs carried infringement warnings.
